sections.text: Real‐world observations of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors as potential treatments for Alzheimer's disease
Abstract
INTRODUCTION

Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonists, sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT‐2) inhibitors, and dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors have potential beneficial effects in Alzheimer's disease (AD).
METHODS

We conducted pharmacoepidemiologic studies using two large‐scale real‐world databases. We fitted covariate‐adjusted Cox models to compare the risks of AD among initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors.
RESULTS

We identified GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation compared to DPP‐4 inhibitors initiation was associated with a reduced risk of AD (hazard ratio [HR] ≤ 0.69 and P value < 0.001) and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation was associated with a reduced risk of AD (HR ≤ 0.67 and P value < 0.001).
DISCUSSION

GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation are associated with a reduced risk of AD. Randomized clinical trials are warranted to validate the causal beneficial effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in AD.
Highlights
Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonists are significantly associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer's disease (AD) compared to dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors.
Sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT‐2) inhibitors are significantly associated with a reduced risk of AD compared to dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors.

Two GLP‐1 receptor agonists (liraglutide and semaglutide) and three SGLT‐2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, and empagliflozin) are associated with a reduced risk of AD in drug‐specific sensitivity analyses.
BACKGROUND

Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and neuroinflammation are linked to the pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonists, sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT‐2) inhibitors, and dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors are second‐line antidiabetic medications. GLP‐1 receptor agonists mimic the action of GLP‐1 to increase insulin release and decrease glucagon release, SGLT‐2 inhibitors inhibit renal glucose reabsorption, and DPP‐4 inhibitors suppress the degradation of GLP‐1 and gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP). Clinically, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors have higher effects on reducing blood glucose and weight than DPP‐4 inhibitors; GLP‐1 receptor agonists are recommended for T2DM patients with prior atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD); and SGLT‐2 inhibitors are recommended for T2DM patients with heart failure and/or chronic kidney disease. In mouse models, all of the GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors may reduce neuroinflammation, amyloid beta (Aβ) accumulation, and tau hyper‐phosphorylation. Additionally, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and DPP‐4 inhibitors may alleviate downregulation of GLP‐1 in the AD brain, and GLP‐1 receptor knockout is related to impaired cognitive function in a mouse model. Moreover, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors may mitigate dysregulations of autophagy and mitophagy, which have been linked to AD in recent studies.

In clinical trials, GLP‐1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide, lixisenatide, and semaglutide) and SGLT‐2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin and empagliflozin) have been or are currently being evaluated in AD and/or PD. For AD, exenatide has demonstrated beneficial effects on cerebral glucose metabolism or extracellular vesicles Aβ42 reduction in two phase 2 trials; semaglutide is under evaluation in two phase 3 trials; and liraglutide, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin are under evaluation in phase 2 trials. For PD, exenatide has shown a beneficial effect on motor ability in two phase 2 trials and is currently being assessed in a phase 3 trial, lixisenatide also showed beneficial effect on motor ability in a phase 2 trial, and liraglutide and semaglutide are currently being evaluated in phase 2 trials. In real‐world US patients, a recent study identifies reduced risks of AD in GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiators and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiators compared to other second‐line diabetic drug users; and additional drug‐specific studies observe reduced risks of AD in exenatide users and semaglutide users. Other real‐world data‐based studies from different countries show mixed relationships involving GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, DPP‐4 inhibitors, AD, and PD. The effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors in AD and PD remain inconclusive in subgroups.

In this study, we comprehensively evaluated the relationships of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors with onset of AD/PD outcomes given their potential neuroprotective effects. We leveraged two large‐scale US real‐world health patient databases. We conducted comparisons between all pairs of drug classes of interest (e.g., GLP‐1 receptor agonists vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, SGLT‐2 inhibitors vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, and GLP‐1 receptor agonists vs. SGLT‐2 inhibitors) with respect to the risks of AD and PD.
METHODS
Real‐world patient databases

We used Optum's de‐identified Clinformatics® Data Mart database (Optum Clinformatics® [2007–2021]) and electronic health record (EHR) data from the Northwestern Medicine Enterprise Data Warehouse (NMEDW [2005–2023]). Optum Clinformatics® data were derived from a database of administrative health claims for members of large commercial and Medicare Advantage health plans, and included demographic variables (e.g., sex, year of birth, and race), enrollment records, diagnosis records, and pharmacy claims. NMEDW data contained EHR data from 11 hospitals in Illinois with comprehensive clinical information, including demographic variables (e.g., sex, year of birth, race, and body mass index [BMI]), diagnosis records, and medication orders. Please see Supplemental Materials S1 in supporting information for additional details about the data sources.
RESEARCH IN CONTEXT

Systematic review: The authors reviewed the literature using traditional methods. Support for efficacy of glucagon‐like peptide‐1 (GLP‐1) receptor agonists and sodium‐glucose cotransporter‐2 (SGLT‐2) inhibitors in treating Alzheimer's disease (AD) has been reported in published non‐clinical studies. Currently, several phase 2 and phase 3 clinical trials are evaluating the efficacy of these agents in AD. Real‐world patient data‐based observations, however, report mixed results for protective roles of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in AD.

Interpretation: GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors were significantly associated with a reduced risk of AD compared to dipeptidyl peptidase‐4 (DPP‐4) inhibitors in two large‐scale US real‐world patient data sources from the Optum Clinformatics® and electronic health records data from Northwestern Medicine Enterprise Data Warehouse.

Future directions: The data support the rationale for current randomized controlled clinical trials on the clinical benefits of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in AD and suggest that further study of the therapeutic benefits of these agents is warranted.
Ascertainment of drug exposure and phenotypes

We generated drug exposure data from pharmacy claims from Optum Clinformatics® data and medication orders from NMEDW data. For the drugs of interest, both data sources included (1) GLP‐1 receptor agonists including albiglutide, dulaglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, lixisenatide, and semaglutide; (2) SGLT‐2 inhibitors including canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, and ertugliflozin; and (3) DPP‐4 inhibitors, including alogliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, and sitagliptin. Additionally, we collected drug exposure data on insulin, metformin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinedione, and other non‐insulin blood glucose–lowering agents including alpha glucosidase inhibitors (i.e., other antidiabetic agents) from both data sources according to the Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical (ATC) classification system (https://www.whocc.no/).

We used subject‐matter expert–derived algorithms to define AD (e.g., International Classification of Diseases [ICD]‐9: 3310 [Alzheimer's disease]; and ICD‐10: F00* [Dementia in Alzheimer's disease] and G30* [Alzheimer's disease]), which had positive predictive value (PPV) = 75% and sensitivity = 71% on identifying AD. We defined PD by ICD‐9 3320 (Parkinson's disease), ICD‐9 3321 (secondary parkinsonism), and ICD‐10 G20 (Parkinson's disease; PPVs: 56%–90%). We used the R package comorbidity and the algorithm derived by Cheng et al. to process data on diagnosis codes, and defined diseases in the Charlson Comorbidity Index, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, and Veterans Affairs Frailty Index (e.g., cerebrovascular disease, congestive heart failure, etc.). We used diagnosis codes from Clinformatics data and BMI from NMEDW data to define weight‐related covariates.
Study design

We targeted initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and/or DPP‐4 inhibitors. For each of the two patient data sources, we derived three cohorts, including (1) initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and/or DPP‐4 inhibitors, (2) initiators of SGLT‐2 inhibitors and/or DPP‐4 inhibitors, and (3) initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and/or SGLT‐2 inhibitors. Further, for each cohort, we also derived two analytical datasets for AD analysis and PD analysis. In each analytical dataset, we defined day 0 as the first initiation date of the drug classes of interest and then defined the initiating drug class according to the exposure record on day 0. We defined the outcomes as days from day 0 to the earliest diagnosis date of AD and PD in the AD and PD datasets, respectively. In other words, the follow‐up time was measured in days. Figure S1 in supporting information illustrates the study design for two drug classes and AD analysis.

We derived six analytical datasets from each data source. Figure S2 in supporting information illustrates the sample flowchart for data preparation. In each dataset, we included individuals with ≥ 60 years of age and initiated one or more of the corresponding two drug classes of interest. We excluded individuals initiated on both drug classes on day 0, and/or diagnosis of acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, cancer, dementia, hemiplegia/paraplegia, and/or other neurological diseases on or before day 0. Additionally, for Clinformatics data, we excluded individuals with < 2 years of continuous enrollment, and/or < 365 days of enrollment prior to day 0. For NMEDW data, we excluded individuals with no outcome and the last observation date < 2 years from day 0. Moreover, we excluded individuals with AD and PD on or before day 0 in the AD and PD datasets, respectively. We defined censoring date as (1) last observation date for individuals initiating a single drug class, and (2) the first initiation date of the second drug class for individuals initiating both drug classes (Figure S1). In other words, we censored individuals without any outcome (e.g., AD and PD) at the earliest of the last observation date or initiation date of the second drug class.

We incorporated covariates that were associated with outcome (e.g., age, sex, race, cerebrovascular disease, and congestive heart failure), exposure (e.g., congestive heart failure, obesity, and renal disease), and commonly used in pharmacoepidemiologic studies. For both Optum Clinformatics® data and NMEDW data, we collected the following baseline covariates (Figure S1): age (60–74 and ≥ 75); sex (female and male); race (White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and unknown); weight‐related covariates (obesity, overweight, under and/or normal, and unknown); and baseline binary covariates (yes/no), including cerebrovascular disease, chronic pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, depression, no diabetes, uncomplicated diabetes, mild liver disease, moderate or severe liver disease, myocardial infarction, peripheral vascular disease, peptic ulcer disease, psychosis, renal disease, rheumatoid disease, insulin exposure, metformin exposure, sulfonylureas exposure, thiazolidinedione exposure, other antidiabetic agent exposure, GLP‐1 receptor agonists exposure, SGLT‐2 inhibitors exposure, and DPP‐4 inhibitors exposure. For Clinformatics data, we collected additional baseline binary covariates, including alcohol use disorder, hypothyroidism, anemia, falls, hearing impairment/loss, and vision comorbidity.
Statistical analyses

We used covariate‐adjusted and index year‐stratified (e.g., stratified by the year of day 0) Cox models to estimate the hazard ratios (HRs), 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs), and P values in all analyses. In overall analyses, covariates in the Cox models included initiating drug classes and all covariates defined in the “study design” section. We then conducted race‐, sex‐, and weight‐specific subgroup analyses. In these subgroup analyses, covariates in the Cox models included initiating drug classes, and all covariates defined in the “study design” section excluding the corresponding subgroup‐specific covariates (e.g., excluding sex as a covariate in sex‐specific subgroup analysis, while all other covariates were adjusted).

We conducted additional sensitivity analyses for AD. First, we conducted sensitivity analyses by using covariate‐adjusted Cox model and individuals with ages between 60 and 74 years. Second, we conducted propensity score (PS)‐matched analyses by using the R package MatchIt (Supplemental Material S2 in supporting information). In short, we controlled all covariates and index year in PS matching. We selected the top 25% matched pairs based on distance of PS between the matched pairs to improve covariate balancing. We used a Cox model to analyze the matched datasets. Third, we exclude individuals with PD prior to day 0, defined PD as a censoring event, and analyzed Optum Clinformatics® data by using covariate‐adjusted Cox model. Fourth, we conducted drug‐specific analyses by replacing the initiating drug classes with initiating drugs in the covariate‐adjust Cox models, in which the initiating drug was derived from the drug exposure record on day 0. Fifth, we defined the outcome as time to AD and related dementias (ADRD; i.e., AD and/or dementia), and analyzed Optum Clinformatics® data by using a covariate‐adjusted Cox model.
RESULTS

We constructed 12 analytical drug cohorts with respect to two data sources (Clinformatics and NMEDW), three comparisons (GLP‐1 receptor agonists vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, SGLT‐2 inhibitors vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, and GLP‐1 receptor agonists vs. SGLT‐2 inhibitors), and two disease outcomes (AD and PD).

In Optum Clinformatics® data analyses, we identified 63,927 initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and 142,470 initiators of DPP‐4 inhibitors for comparing the AD risk between the two drug classes; and 58,866 initiators of SGLT‐2 inhibitors and 142,388 initiators of DPP‐4 inhibitors for comparing the AD risk between the two drug classes. Table 1 presents the demographics of GLP‐1 receptor agonists versus DPP‐4 inhibitors cohorts and SGLT‐2 inhibitors versus DPP‐4 inhibitors cohorts for AD analyses derived from Optum Clinformatics®. In NMEDW data analyses, we identified 6010 initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and 9252 initiators of DPP‐4 inhibitors for comparing the AD risk between the two drug classes; and 4660 initiators of SGLT‐2 inhibitors and 8865 initiators of DPP‐4 inhibitors for comparing the AD risk between the two drug classes. Tables S1 and S2 in supporting information present the demographics of all 12 drug cohorts derived from Optum Clinformatics® and NMEDW. Table S3 in supporting information presents the demographics of PS‐matched datasets. Table S4 in supporting information presents summary statistics of lengths of follow‐up and AD cases.

GLP‐1 receptor agonists versus DPP‐4 inhibitors: associations with AD

As shown in Figure 1A,B, GLP‐1 receptor agonists (a pool drug cohort of albiglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, lixisenatide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide) initiation was significantly associated with a reduced risk of AD compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation in overall analyses (0.54 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.69 and P values < 0.001), female subgroup analyses (0.33 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.66 and P values < 0.001), White subgroup analyses (0.49 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.67 and P values < 0.001), and obese subgroup analyses (0.35 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.72 and P values ≤ 0.002). For the Optum Clinformatics® database (Figure 1A), GLP‐1 receptor agonists initiation compared to DPP‐4 inhibitors initiation was significantly associated with a lower risk of AD in male, Hispanic, and Black subgroup analyses (0.72 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.77 and P values ≤ 0.031). In additional sensitivity analyses, GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation was associated with a reduced risk of AD in individuals with ages between 60 and 74 years, and PS‐matched analyses (Figure 2); in individuals without PD at baseline and considering PD as a censoring event (Figure S3 in supporting information); as well as associated with a reduced risk of ADRD (Figure S4 in supporting information). In drug‐specific sensitivity analyses, liraglutide initiation and semaglutide initiation were significantly associated with reduced risks of AD compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation (0.23 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.69 and P values ≤ 0.012; Figure S5 in supporting information).

SGLT‐2 inhibitors versus DPP‐4 inhibitors: associations with AD

As shown in Figure 3, SGLT‐2 inhibitors (a pool drug cohort of canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, ertugliflozin) initiation were associated with a reduced risk of AD compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation in overall analyses (0.32 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.67 and P values < 0.001), female subgroup analyses (0.31 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.76 and P values ≤0.002), male subgroup analyses (0.31 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.55 and P values < 0.001), White subgroup analyses (0.26 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.64 and P values < 0.001), obese subgroup analyses (0.31 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.70 and P values ≤ 0.008), and overweight subgroup analyses (0.36 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.52 and P values ≤0.021). For the Optum Clinformatics® database (Figure 3A), SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation was associated with a lower risk of AD in the Hispanic subgroup analysis (HR = 0.73 and P value = 0.035). In addition, for an independent NMEDW EHR patient database, SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation was associated with a lower risk of AD in normal weight subgroup analyses as well (HR = 0.25 and P = 0.016, Figure 3B). In additional sensitivity analyses, SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation was associated with a reduced risk of AD in individuals with ages between 60 and 74 years, and PS‐matched analyses (Figure 4); and in individuals without PD at baseline and considering PD as a censoring event (Figure S6 in supporting information); as well as associated with a reduced risk of ADRD (Figure S7 in supporting information). In drug‐specific sensitivity analyses, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin, or empagliflozin exposures were associated with reduced risks of AD compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation (0.24 ≤ HRs ≤ 0.74 and P values ≤ 0.036, Figure S8 in supporting information).

GLP‐1 receptor agonists versus SGLT‐2 inhibitors: associations with AD

For GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation versus SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation, no consistent differences in AD were observed from both data sources in overall analyses and sensitivity analyses (Figures S9–S11 in supporting information).
Other results

For PD, no consistent differences were observed in all comparisons (GLP‐1 receptor agonist vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, SGLT‐2 inhibitors vs. DPP‐4 inhibitors, and GLP‐1 receptor agonists vs. SGLT‐2 inhibitors; Figures S12–S15 in supporting information). Full results of Cox models in overall analyses of Clinformatics data are presented in Tables S5–S7 in supporting information.
DISCUSSION

Our study provides real‐world evidence on the comparative effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors for AD onset. We find that GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation are significantly associated with a reduced risk of AD compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation from two large‐scale real‐world patient data sources, including the US nationwide Optum Clinformatics® database and Illinois‐based (i.e., a US state–based) EHR data from the NMEDW.

Our findings are in agreement with and enhance other real‐world observations on GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and AD. In our study, compared to DPP‐4 inhibitor initiation, we find HRs ≤ 0.69 (P values ≤ 0.001 [Figure 1]) for GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation. In a recently published study using Florida‐based (i.e., a US state–based) EHR data, compared to other second line antidiabetic drugs (e.g., DPP‐4 inhibitors, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, etc.) initiation, the HRs were ≤ 0.67 (all P values < 0.05) for GLP‐1 receptor agonist initiation and SGLT‐2 inhibitor initiation. Thus, the associations involving GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and AD are consistent between the US nationwide administrative claim data and two sets of US state–based EHR data. Additionally, a US Medicare data–based study found one GLP‐1 receptor agonist (exenatide) is associated with a lower risk of AD in a dose–response model, and a US nationwide EHR‐based study found another GLP‐1 receptor agonist (semaglutide) exposure is associated with a lower risk of AD compared to other antidiabetic drugs (or drug classes) exposure. Moreover, SGLT‐2 inhibitor exposure is associated with a lower risk of AD in Hongkong‐ and Ontario‐based EHR data. Our study also provides subgroup‐specific drug responses in AD for GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors compared to DPP‐4 inhibitors. GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors compared to DPP‐4 inhibitors have a consistent lower risk of AD in female, White, and obese subgroup analyses (Figures 1 and 3), which suggests a low heterogeneity of the potential beneficial effect in these subgroups.

Several possible mechanisms of action of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in potential treatment of AD have been proposed. While all of the GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors may reduce neuroinflammation, Aβ accumulation, and tau hyper‐phosphorylation in mouse models, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors have a higher permeability across the blood–brain barrier than DPP‐4 inhibitors. Additionally, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors could improve cognition by reducing vascular damage and neuronal loss, and mitigating dysregulation of autophagy and/or mitophagy related to AD. In summary, our real‐world data findings (Figures 1, 2, 3, 4) are supported by various existing preclinical studies. The detailed mechanisms of action of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in potential treatment of AD should be investigated further.

For patients requiring a GLP‐1 receptor agonist, a SGLT‐2 inhibitor, or a DPP‐4 inhibitor, considerations on drug selection are based on heart and kidney conditions, required intensity of blood glucose and/or weight management, and risks of adverse events. Given real‐world observations from our study and other studies, and preclinical findings, additional considerations on drug selection might be given to risk of AD. For instance, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors might be recommended to patients with risk factors for AD, if the observations are validated.

We acknowledge several potential limitations in the current study. First, the Clinformatics data are derived from US individuals with commercial and/or Medicare supplemental insurance plans and the NMEDW data primarily consist of individuals encountered with Northwestern Medicine. Our analyses are targeted on individuals initiating GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and/or DPP‐4 inhibitors. Although the patient data we used include older individuals with diverse demographics (e.g., geographical regions, sex, ethnicity, and races), our current findings might not be generalizable to individuals without insurance; retirees without a Medicare supplemental insurance plan; as well as individuals without GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and/or DPP‐4 inhibitors initiation. Second, the results could be subject to unmeasured and/or residual confounding effects related to socioeconomic status (SES); education level, smoking status, blood glucose level, other lab records, severity of diabetes, severity of other comorbidity (e.g., heart and kidney diseases), COVID‐19 infection, genotypes (e.g., apolipoprotein E genotype), health care–seeking behaviors, patterns of health care, missing data on weight, and life expectancy; as well as potential violations of model assumptions. Certain AD‐related patient characteristics have different prevalence between users of GLP‐1 receptor agonists, SGLT‐2 inhibitors, and DPP‐4 inhibitors. For instance, while all drug classes are approved second‐line therapy for T2DM, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors are also recommended for preventing and/or managing heart and kidney diseases, and have higher blood glucose and weight‐lowering effects than DPP‐4 inhibitors. In our datasets, obesity is more frequent in initiators of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors than in initiators of DPP‐4 inhibitors. Obesity is a risk factor for COVID‐19 infection and mortality, and COVID‐19 increases the risk of mortality. Despite the fact that obesity is controlled in Cox models, its relationships to COVID‐19, life expectancy, and onset of AD are not fully adjusted. Additionally, while renal disease has a similar frequency between initiators of all three drug classes, severity of renal disease is not controlled, and is related to both AD and life expectancy. Moreover, health care–seeking behavior and patterns of health care might also relate to the detection of AD, and GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors users might have a higher frequency of health exams related to heart and kidney conditions than DPP‐4 inhibitors users. Third, neurological exams, cognitive tests, and brain images are also not included in the current study and biological confirmation of the diagnosis of AD was not available. Given these limitations, while GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors demonstrate potential neuroprotective effects and potential brain penetrant properties, our findings cannot be interpreted as causality. Several ongoing interventional clinical trials are currently investigating the effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors in populations of patients with AD.

In summary, GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors may offer potential prevention or treatment effects for AD. Randomized controlled trials in diverse populations are highly warranted to further test clinical beneficial effects of GLP‐1 receptor agonists and SGLT‐2 inhibitors.
